\subsection{What a resting vertex can gain}
\label{sec:lane}

Throughout this subsection $G$ is a stopping SSG, $C:=\Vmax\cup\Vmin$, and for
$u\in C$ and $a\in\{0,1\}$ we write $(p^{u,a},q^{u,a})$ for the \emph{first
passage law} of the $a$-th action of $u$ onto $C\cup\{t_1\}$: $p^{u,a}_w$ is the
probability that the token, having left $u$ by that edge, next meets a
controlled vertex at $w$, and $q^{u,a}$ the probability that it reaches $t_1$
before any controlled vertex. Only average vertices lie strictly between two
controlled vertices, so $(p^{u,a},q^{u,a})$ is a datum of the \emph{graph},
independent of both strategies, and every value vector satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{lane:eq-fp}
  \val_\sigma(u)\;=\;\sum_{w\in C}p^{u,\sigma(u)}_w\val_\sigma(w)+q^{u,\sigma(u)}
  \qquad(u\in\Vmax),
\end{equation}
because $\val_\sigma$ is a fixed point of $T_\sigma$ and is therefore the mean of
its successors at every average vertex. The same identity holds at $u\in\Vmin$
with $\sigma(u)$ replaced by any Min best response to $\sigma$. Write
$W(u,a):=\{w\in C\setminus\{u\}:p^{u,a}_w>0\}$, the \emph{read set} of the
action, and call $u\in\Vmax$ \emph{at rest} at $\sigma$ if $u\notin S_\sigma$.

\begin{lemma}[Rise bound]\label{lane:rise-bound}
Let $G$ be stopping, let $\sigma,\sigma'$ be Max strategies with
$\val_{\sigma'}\ge\val_\sigma$ pointwise, and let $u\in\Vmax$ be at rest at
$\sigma$. Put $b:=\sigma'(u)$. Then
\[
  \val_{\sigma'}(u)-\val_\sigma(u)\;\le\;
  \max_{w\in W(u,b)}\bigl(\val_{\sigma'}(w)-\val_\sigma(w)\bigr),
\]
the maximum over the empty set being $0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write $x:=\val_\sigma$, $y:=\val_{\sigma'}$, $\Delta_w:=y(w)-x(w)\ge0$,
$M:=\max_{w\in W(u,b)}\Delta_w\ge0$, $p:=p^{u,b}$, $q:=q^{u,b}$. Being at rest
means that \emph{both} actions of $u$ have value at most $x(u)$ under $x$; for
the action $b$ this reads, by \eqref{lane:eq-fp} applied to a strategy taking
$b$ at $u$,
\[
  p_u\,x(u)+\sum_{w\ne u}p_w\,x(w)+q\;\le\;x(u).
\]
Since $\sigma'(u)=b$, \eqref{lane:eq-fp} gives
$y(u)=p_uy(u)+\sum_{w\ne u}p_wy(w)+q$. Subtracting, and using
$\sum_{w\ne u}p_w\le 1-p_u$,
\[
  (1-p_u)\bigl(y(u)-x(u)\bigr)\;\le\;\sum_{w\ne u}p_w\Delta_w\;\le\;(1-p_u)M .
\]
Finally $p_u<1$: if $p_u=1$ the action $b$ would return to $u$ with probability
one, so $\{u\}$ together with the average vertices on those paths would be a
trap, contradicting stopping (\Cref{lem:trapchar}).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[No overtaking]\label{lane:no-overtake}
Let $\sigma_0,\sigma_1,\dots$ be a run of improving switches on a stopping SSG,
$u\in\Vmax$, and let $b$ be an action of $u$ with $W(u,b)=\{w\}$ a single
controlled vertex. If $u\notin S_{\sigma_t}$ and $\sigma_{t'}(u)=b$ for some
$t'>t$, then
\[
  \val_{\sigma_{t'}}(u)-\val_{\sigma_{t'}}(w)\;\le\;
  \val_{\sigma_t}(u)-\val_{\sigma_t}(w).
\]
In particular, if $\val_{\sigma_t}(u)\le\val_{\sigma_t}(w)$ then
$\val_{\sigma_{t'}}(u)\le\val_{\sigma_{t'}}(w)$ for every such $t'$: a vertex
that is once at rest never overtakes the single vertex its action reads.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[The peak of an interval sits on $S_t$]\label{lane:peak-source}
Let $G$ be stopping and $\sigma_0,\dots,\sigma_L$ an all-switches run. For all
$0\le t<t'\le L$,
\[
  \max_{v\in V}\bigl(\val_{\sigma_{t'}}(v)-\val_{\sigma_t}(v)\bigr)
  \;=\;\max_{v\in S_t}\bigl(\val_{\sigma_{t'}}(v)-\val_{\sigma_t}(v)\bigr).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
``$\ge$'' is trivial. Put $\Delta:=\val_{\sigma_{t'}}-\val_{\sigma_t}\ge0$
(\Cref{lem:switch}) and $A:=C\setminus S_t$. The computation in the proof of
\Cref{lane:rise-bound} gives, for every $u\in A\cap\Vmax$ with
$b=\sigma_{t'}(u)$,
\[
  \Delta_u\;\le\;\sum_{w\ne u}\tilde p_w\Delta_w,\qquad
  \tilde p_w:=\frac{p^{u,b}_w}{1-p^{u,b}_u},\qquad \sum_{w\ne u}\tilde p_w\le1 ,
\]
and the same inequality holds at $u\in\Vmin$ with $b$ the action of a Min best
response to $\sigma_t$, because there $\val_{\sigma_{t'}}(u)$ is a minimum over
actions, hence at most the value of that particular one, while
$\val_{\sigma_t}(u)$ equals it. Collecting these rows, $\Delta|_A\le
Q\,\Delta|_A+R\,\Delta|_{S_t}$ with $[Q\ R]$ substochastic. The matrix
$\tilde P$ is the jump chain of the transient substochastic $P$ obtained by
deleting self-loops and renormalising, and $I-\tilde P=(I-D)^{-1}(I-P)$ with
$D=\operatorname{diag}(p_{uu})$, so $\tilde P$ is transient too and so is its
submatrix $Q$. Hence $\Delta|_A\le(I-Q)^{-1}R\,\Delta|_{S_t}$, and
$(I-Q)^{-1}R\mathbf 1\le\mathbf 1$ (it is the vector of probabilities of ever
leaving $A$ into $S_t$). Therefore $\max_A\Delta\le\max_{S_t}\Delta$. Values at
average vertices are means of values at $C\cup\{t_0,t_1\}$ and the sinks have
$\Delta=0$, so the maximum over $V$ is the maximum over $C$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{lane:peak-vs-peak-law}
\Cref{lane:peak-source} is sharper than \Cref{thm:peak-law} in the direction
that matters for lower-bound constructions: the peak of $\val_{\sigma_{t'}}-
\val_{\sigma_t}$ lies on the set switched \emph{at the beginning} of the
interval, for every later $t'$ at once, and $|S_t|\le|\Vmax|$. Taking $t=0$ and
$t'=L$: the whole improvement of the run is realised at a vertex that is
strictly switchable at the very first round.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Verification]\label{lane:verify-laws}
All three statements were verified in exact rational arithmetic.
\Cref{lane:rise-bound}: $74\,232$ instances $(\text{game},\sigma,\sigma',u)$ on
random one-player normal forms with $m\le6$, and a further $10\,933$ at the SSG
level on random stopping games with $3$--$8$ non-sinks, both players present
(so both the $\Vmax$ and the $\Vmin$ rows of the proof are exercised); no
violation. \Cref{lane:peak-source}: all pairs $t<t'$ of all-switches runs from
every start, $5\,572$ pairs on one-player normal forms and $283$ on random
two-player stopping games; no violation. \Cref{lane:autonomy} below: $610$
projected switch sequences over all autonomous $U$ with $|U|\le4$; no
violation. Files \texttt{t\_rise.py}, \texttt{t\_laws.py}; transcript
\texttt{VERIFY.log}.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Autonomy: a self-contained module is never re-run}

\begin{definition}[Autonomous module]\label{lane:autonomous}
$U\subseteq\Vmax$ is \emph{autonomous} in a one-player SSG $G$ if
$W(u,a)\subseteq U$ for every $u\in U$ and both $a$ --- equivalently, every
path leaving a vertex of $U$ meets a sink or a vertex of $U$ before any other
Max vertex. Then $G|_U$, the sub-SSG induced on $U$ together with the average
vertices met on those paths, is a stopping SSG in its own right (its vertices
have the same out-edges as in $G$, and a trap of $G|_U$ would be a trap of
$G$).
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Autonomy law]\label{lane:autonomy}
Let $G$ be a one-player stopping SSG, $U$ autonomous, and
$\sigma_0,\dots,\sigma_L$ an all-switches run with switch sets $S_0,\dots,S_{L-1}$.
Then $t\mapsto S_t\cap U$ is the switch sequence of the all-switches run of the
stopping game $G|_U$ from $\sigma_0|_U$, padded with $\emptyset$; in particular
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),leftmargin=2.2em]
\item once $S_t\cap U=\emptyset$, $S_{t'}\cap U=\emptyset$ for all $t'\ge t$;
\item the nonempty sets among $S_0\cap U,\dots,S_{L-1}\cap U$ are pairwise
      distinct;
\item $\#\{t:S_t\cap U\ne\emptyset\}\le h^\ast(|U|)$, and
      $\le h^\ast_{HK}(|U|)$ if moreover $G|_U$ is nondegenerate.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By \eqref{lane:eq-fp} and autonomy the restriction $\val_\sigma|_U$ solves the
linear system of $G|_U$ determined by $\sigma|_U$ alone, so
$\val_\sigma|_U=\val_{\sigma|_U}^{G|_U}$. Hence $S_\sigma\cap U$
depends only on $\sigma|_U$ and equals $S^{G|_U}_{\sigma|_U}$. Therefore the
projection of the run is exactly the all-switches run of $G|_U$, which stops
when its switch set is empty --- and then stays put, giving (a). (b) is
\Cref{cor:law-u} applied to $G|_U$, and (c) is \Cref{cor:ceiling-general}
together with \Cref{prop:oneplayer-lp}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Modules do not add up]\label{lane:modules}
If $\Vmax=U_1\uplus\dots\uplus U_r$ with every $U_i$ autonomous, then the
all-switches run of $G$ has length $\max_i L_i$, where $L_i$ is the length of
the run of $G|_{U_i}$ from $\sigma_0|_{U_i}$. Placing gadgets side by side
therefore never lengthens a run; a gadget that is to be run twice must have an
action reading a vertex outside itself.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}\label{lane:autonomy-vs-isolated}
\Cref{lane:autonomy} is the module form of \Cref{allswlower:lem-isolated}(ii),
which is its case ``$U$ is switched alone in one round''. What it adds is that
the impossibility of a reset is not a property of a single quiet round: an
autonomous module can never repeat \emph{any} of its own switch patterns, so
no amount of external stimulation can make a self-contained lane oscillate,
and \Cref{cor:law-u} bites inside the module even when the ambient switched
sets are all distinct.
\end{remark}

\subsection{The impedance denominator buys nothing}

\Cref{thm:impedance} says that the rise produced by switching $u$ is
$(f(b)-f(a))/(1-h(b\!\to\!u))$, and $1-h$ can be $2^{-\Theta(N)}$; the natural
hope --- and the reason this route was opened --- is that a switch delayed long
enough can therefore gain far more than the event that triggered it. It cannot.

\begin{proposition}[Amplification cancels]\label{lane:impedance-cancels}
Let $G$ be a stopping SSG, $\sigma_0,\dots,\sigma_L$ an all-switches run,
$u\in\Vmax$ at rest at $\sigma_t$, and suppose $u\in S_{t'}$ for some $t'\ge t$
with $b:=\bar\sigma_{t'}(u)$ the action it switches to. Let
$h:=p^{u,b}_u=h(b\!\to\!u)$, so that \Cref{thm:impedance} writes the rise at
$u$ in that round as $\bigl(\val_{\sigma_{t'}}(b)-\val_{\sigma_{t'}}(a)\bigr)/(1-h)$.
Then
\[
  \val_{\sigma_{t'+1}}(u)-\val_{\sigma_t}(u)\;\le\;
  \max_{w\in W(u,b)}\bigl(\val_{\sigma_{t'+1}}(w)-\val_{\sigma_t}(w)\bigr).
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\Cref{lane:rise-bound} with $\sigma=\sigma_t$, $\sigma'=\sigma_{t'+1}$; note
$\sigma_{t'+1}(u)=b$ and $\val_{\sigma_{t'+1}}\ge\val_{\sigma_t}$ by
\Cref{lem:switch}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The rise accounting]\label{lane:accounting}
The two statements are consistent and say different things. The \emph{gap}
$\val(b)-\val(a)$ that makes $u$ switchable is indeed damped by the loop: if
$b$ returns to $u$ with probability $h$, then before the switch
$\val(b)=h\val(u)+(1-h)\ell$ where $\ell$ is the value of $b$ conditioned on
not returning, so the gap is $(1-h)(\ell-\val(u))$, while the rise is
$\ell-\val(u)$ --- this is \Cref{allswlower:cor-selfread}, and the ratio
$1/(1-h)$ is unbounded. What \Cref{lane:impedance-cancels} adds is that
$\ell-\val(u)$ itself is bounded by the largest rise, over the whole waiting
period, among the vertices $b$ reads. So a delayed switch may gain far more
than the \emph{gap} that triggered it, and never more than the \emph{rise} of
its trigger. The premise on which this route was opened is therefore false in
the form in which it was stated, and true only in the weaker form ``more than
the gap''.

Reconciliation with \Cref{cor:no-return} for a vertex switched twice. Suppose
$u\in S_{t}$ and $u\in S_{t''}$ with $\sigma_{t''+1}(u)=\sigma_t(u)$, i.e.\ $u$
returns to an old action. By \Cref{lem:switch} $\val(u)$ rises strictly at each
of the two switches, so the second switch does have a rise; by
\Cref{cor:no-return} applied to $t<t''+1$ the set $S_t$ must contain a vertex
at which $\sigma_t$ and $\sigma_{t''+1}$ differ, and that vertex is not $u$, so
$S_t\ne\{u\}$ --- a vertex switched \emph{alone} never switches again
(\Cref{allswlower:lem-isolated}(i)). The size of the second rise is then
governed by \Cref{lane:rise-bound} applied from any round in $(t,t'')$ at which
$u$ was at rest: it is at most the largest rise, over that interval, of the
vertices the restored action reads. Nothing in the two-switch pattern is
paid for by the escape denominator.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[An exit chain never passes its driver's read point]\label{lane:exit-chain}
Let $G$ be a one-player stopping SSG and let $l_1,\dots,l_n,d\in\Vmax$ be
distinct. Suppose that for each $i$ one action $b_i$ of $l_i$ has
$W(l_i,b_i)\subseteq\{l_{i-1}\}$, where $l_0:=d$, and that both actions of $d$
have $W(d,\cdot)\subseteq\{l_1,\dots,l_j\}$ for some $j\le n$. Let
$\sigma_0,\sigma_1,\dots$ be a run of improving switches and suppose that at
some round $t$
\[
  \sigma_t(l_i)=b_i\ (1\le i\le j)\qquad\text{and}\qquad d\notin S_{\sigma_t}.
\]
Then for every $t'>t$ at which $\sigma_{t'}(l_i)=b_i$ for all $i\le j$ we have
$\sigma_{t'}(d)=\sigma_t(d)$ and $\val_{\sigma_{t'}}=\val_{\sigma_t}$ on
$\{d,l_1,\dots,l_j\}$. Consequently, as soon as one of
$d,l_1,\dots,l_j$ has strictly raised its value since round $t$, the
configuration $(\sigma(l_1),\dots,\sigma(l_j))=(b_1,\dots,b_j)$ never occurs
again.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Put $W:=\{d,l_1,\dots,l_j\}$ and, for each action $a$ of $d$,
$\pi_a:=(d\mapsto a,\ l_i\mapsto b_i)$. Every vertex reachable from $\pi_a(W)$
without meeting $W$ again is an average vertex or a sink, so $(W,\pi_a)$ is a
closed configuration in the sense of \Cref{prop:closed-now-or-never}. Let $a$
be the action of $d$ \emph{not} taken at $\sigma_t$. Then
$W_t=\{v\in W:\sigma_t(v)\ne\pi_a(v)\}=\{d\}$ is nonempty and meets
$S_{\sigma_t}$ not at all, so \Cref{prop:closed-now-or-never}(b) gives
$\sigma_{t'}|_W\ne\pi_a$ for every $t'\ge t$. Hence if all $l_i$, $i\le j$,
are at $b_i$ at $\sigma_{t'}$, then $\sigma_{t'}(d)=\sigma_t(d)$, i.e.\
$\sigma_{t'}|_W=\sigma_t|_W$, and since $W$ is closed for that configuration
too, the values on $W$ are the same vector $\lambda_W$ at both rounds.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The delay/reach budget of a two-phase lane]\label{lane:budget}
This is exactly what stops the construction the route set out to build. Take
the lane $l_i\to(l_{i+1},\ \text{exit}_i)$ with $\text{exit}_i$ reading
$l_{i-1}$ and $l_0=d$ a driver whose idle action is a constant and whose other
action reads $l_j$. Then:
\emph{(i)} the driver cannot fire before the first (``continue'') wave has
reached $l_j$, i.e.\ before round $k-j+1$, because until then $\val(l_j)$ has
not moved; and
\emph{(ii)} by \Cref{lane:exit-chain} the second (``exit'') wave, which
travels $l_1,l_2,\dots$, can never reach $l_j$, so it makes at most $j-1$
switches.
Delay plus reach is therefore at most $k+1$, whatever $j$: the two-phase lane
has an all-switches run of at most $k+O(1)$ rounds, i.e.\ no better than the
plain lane it was built from. This was confirmed by an exact scan over the
family (masses, rewards, both read points, all parameters dyadic with
denominator $256$): the longest run found at $k=5$, $|\Vmax|=7$, is $7$ rounds
(\texttt{t\_lane2.py}). Replacing the single driver by drivers reading
mixtures of the whole lane removes the closed set --- and therefore removes
this obstruction --- but the same scan over that family
(\texttt{rl.py}, $k\le5$) also found nothing longer than $|\Vmax|$.
\end{remark}

\subsection{How cheap a linear lane is, and what the value grid allows}

The lane of \Cref{fs14:lane-def} spends $\Theta(\log k)$ average vertices per
Max vertex to make its $k$ exit values distinct. None of that is needed.

\begin{definition}[Three linear lanes]\label{lane:three}
For $k\ge2$:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.6em]
\item $RC(k)$ (\emph{reachability chain}): $\Vmax=\{v_1,\dots,v_k\}$, no average
vertex, $v_i\to(v_{i+1},t_0)$ for $i<k$ and $v_k\to(t_1,t_0)$.
\item $ALH(k)$ (\emph{all-half chain}): $\Vmax=\{p_1,\dots,p_k\}$, one average
vertex $h\to(t_1,t_0)$, and $p_i\to(p_{i+1},h)$ with $p_{k+1}:=t_1$.
\item $CL(k)$ (\emph{damped lane}): $\Vmax=\{l_1,\dots,l_k\}$,
$\Vavg=\{g_1,\dots,g_k\}$, $l_i\to(l_{i+1},g_i)$ with $l_{k+1}:=t_1$,
$g_i\to(l_{i-1},t_0)$ and $g_1\to(t_1,t_0)$.
\end{itemize}
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}\label{lane:linear}
All three are one-player and stopping, and from the start that takes the second
listed action everywhere the all-switches run switches exactly one vertex per
round, in the order $k,k-1,\dots,1$, and halts at the optimum $w^\ast\equiv1$
on $\Vmax$. Hence
\[
  RC(k):\ N=k+2,\ a=0,\ L=N-2;\qquad
  ALH(k):\ N=k+3,\ a=1,\ L=N-3;\qquad
  CL(k):\ N=2k+2,\ a=k,\ L=\tfrac{N-2}2 .
\]
$RC$ and $ALH$ have $\binom k2$ tied incidences along the run, $CL$ has none;
all three are nevertheless degenerate as orientations of the $k$-cube, the tied
incidences of $CL(k)$ over the whole cube being $0,2,12,46,144$ for
$k=2,\dots,6$, so \Cref{thm:flat-resolution} rather than
\Cref{prop:allsw-auso} is what makes their runs bottom-antipodal walks, and
the Holt--Klee ceiling of \Cref{prop:oneplayer-lp} does not apply to them.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Stopping: in $RC$ the graph on $\Vmax$ is acyclic, in $ALH$ and $CL$ every
average vertex has $t_0$ among its successors, so the greatest trap is empty
(\Cref{lem:trapchar}).
$RC$: under the all-$t_0$ strategy every $\val(v_i)=0$; for $i<k$ the other
option is $\val(v_{i+1})=0$, a tie, and all-switches keeps ties, while $v_k$
sees $\val(t_1)=1>0$. Inductively after $r$ rounds $v_{k-r+1},\dots,v_k$ have
value $1$ and the rest $0$, so exactly $v_{k-r}$ switches. Since a vertex's
value is $1$ after it switches, it never switches again.
$ALH$: identical with $0$ replaced by $\tfrac12=\val(h)$ and $1$ by
$\val(t_1)$.
$CL$: under the all-exit strategy $\val(g_1)=\tfrac12$ and
$\val(g_i)=\tfrac12\val(l_{i-1})$, so $\val(l_i)=2^{-i}$; for $i<k$ the other
option is $\val(l_{i+1})=2^{-(i+1)}<2^{-i}$ --- strictly smaller, so no tie and
no switch --- while $l_k$ sees $1>2^{-k}$. After $r$ rounds
$l_{k-r+1},\dots,l_k$ continue with value $1$ and $l_i=2^{-i}$ for $i\le k-r$,
so exactly $l_{k-r}$ switches; and $l_i$ switching to continue only lowers
$\val(g_{i+1})$ to $\tfrac12<1$, so nothing switches back.
The tie counts are the pairs $(i,r)$ with $i<k-r$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The value grid bounds the run]\label{lane:grid}
Let $G$ be a stopping SSG with $m=|\Vmax|$ and $a=|\Vavg|$, and let
$D(a):=\bigl|\{p/q\in[0,1]:1\le q\le 2^{a}\}\bigr|$ be the number of points of
the grid of \Cref{lem:denominator-sharp}. Then every all-switches run satisfies
\[
  L\;\le\;\sum_{v\in\Vmax}n_v\;\le\;m\,\bigl(D(a)-1\bigr),
\]
where $n_v$ is the number of rounds at which $v$ switches. In particular
$L\le m$ when $a=0$ (grid $\{0,1\}$) and $L\le 2m$ when $a=1$ (grid
$\{0,\tfrac12,1\}$).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Each round of the run switches a nonempty set, so $L\le\sum_v n_v$. If $v$
switches at rounds $t_1<\dots<t_{n_v}$ then by \Cref{lem:switch}
$\val_{\sigma_{t_1}}(v)<\val_{\sigma_{t_1+1}}(v)\le\val_{\sigma_{t_2}}(v)<\dots$,
so $v$ takes at least $n_v+1$ distinct values along the run, all on the grid.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{lane:rc-optimal}
$RC(k)$ is optimal among one-player stopping SSGs with no average vertex: there
$L\le|\Vmax|=N-2$, attained. A one-player family with $L>N-2$ must therefore
have $a\ge1$ and must switch some vertex more than once.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}\label{lane:linear-state}
$RC$, $ALH$ and $CL$ all improve on \Cref{fs14:lane-def}, whose $N$ is
$\Theta(k\log k)$ for the same run length $k$; $RC(k)$ is the extreme point,
$L=N-2$, and it is elementary (it is Howard's rule on a deterministic
shortest-path MDP and should be attributed as folklore). $CL(k)$ is the
cheapest lane with no tie along its run. None is superlinear, and by
\Cref{lane:autonomy} none can be made so by iteration: $\Vmax$ is autonomous in
each, so the whole game is a single module and no re-run is possible. Note that
a lane whose $k$ exit values are pairwise distinct needs $k-2$ average vertices
merely to hold those values, so $N\ge2k$: within \emph{that} sub-family $CL$ is
optimal, and the way $RC$ and $ALH$ beat it is precisely by making all the exit
values equal and living on the ties, which is legitimate because all-switches
keeps ties (and is why those two families are degenerate).
\end{remark}

\subsection{Binarisation of a multi-action state}

\begin{lemma}[A Max tree is an $\arg\max$ with logarithmic lag]\label{lane:tree}
Let $s$ be a state with $r\ge2$ actions and let $T_s$ be a rooted binary tree
of $r-1$ fresh Max vertices whose $r$ leaves are the actions of $s$ (each leaf
edge carrying that action's first passage law). If the values of the $r$
actions do not change during $d:=\lceil\log_2 r\rceil$ consecutive rounds of an
all-switches run, then at the end of those rounds the root of $T_s$ selects a
leaf of maximal value, and the value of the root equals $\max_i\val(A_i)$.
The cost is $r-1$ Max vertices and no average vertices.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Induction on the height. A vertex at height $1$ compares its two leaves and
after one round selects the larger. If every vertex at height $\le j$ selects
the maximum of its subtree after $j$ rounds, then a vertex $v$ at height $j+1$
sees, from round $j$ on, the two subtree maxima as its children's values, and
switches if the other is strictly larger; after one further round it selects
the larger of the two, i.e.\ the maximum of its subtree. Ties are kept, which
is harmless since either choice attains the maximum.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[The lag is real]\label{lane:tree-lag}
Take $\mathrm{Lane}(3)$ with exits $\tfrac78,\tfrac34,\tfrac58$ and add
$u=\max(l_1,l_2)$, $p=\max(u,l_3)$; realised as an honest SSG this is $15$
vertices ($5$ Max, $8$ average, $2$ sinks), stopping, and the normal form is
verified from the graph. From the strategy ``all three lane vertices exit,
$u\mapsto l_1$, $p\mapsto u$'' the all-switches run is three rounds, and at
round $1$ the best leaf is worth $1$ while the root $p$ is worth $\tfrac78$:
the root is strictly behind. (\texttt{tree.py}; exact arithmetic.)
\end{example}

\begin{remark}[What a binarisation of the published counters would need]
\label{lane:binarise}
From memory, unchecked against the sources. Fearnley (ICALP 2010) gives an MDP
on which Howard's rule takes $2^{\Omega(n)}$ iterations under the total- and
average-reward criteria; its bit state $b_i$ has $2i+O(1)$ actions (a
probabilistic self-loop $a_i$, the states $x_i,y_i$, and one action into each
of the $2i$ states of a deceleration lane), and each lane state has three
actions, so the instance has $\Theta(n^2)$ states and $\Theta(n^2)$ actions.
Friedmann (LMCS 2011) gives the analogous parity/mean-payoff/discounted/SSG
family, with $d_i$ of out-degree $2i+O(1)$ and $r,s$ of out-degree $n+1$.
Christ and Yannakakis (STOC 2023) do the same for reachability MDPs. Hansen
and Zwick (2010) give $\Omega(n^2)$ with $\Theta(n)$ actions. Melekopoglou and
Condon (1994) is the only two-action lower bound and it is for the
\emph{least-index} rule. Mukherjee and Kalyanakrishnan (ICAPS 2025) record that
for a constant number of actions per state the best known lower bound for
Howard's rule is linear.

Two of the three ingredients binarise at polynomial cost.
\emph{Selection}: \Cref{lane:tree} replaces an $r$-action state by $r-1$ binary
Max vertices, so Fearnley's $\Theta(n^2)$ actions become $\Theta(n^2)$ Max
vertices --- polynomial. \emph{Delay}: a chain of $d$ Max vertices, each with
its second action a constant, transmits a value change in exactly $d$ rounds
(\Cref{lane:three} is the extreme case), so a delay of $d$ rounds costs $d$
vertices, and Fearnley's total delay budget $\sum_i(2i+1)=\Theta(n^2)$ is
affordable. What does \emph{not} transfer is the \emph{timing}: by
\Cref{lane:tree} the selection at a state is correct only $\lceil\log_2 r\rceil$
rounds after its action values settle, and \Cref{lane:tree-lag} shows the root
is strictly behind while they move --- which in the counters they do, every
iteration, by design. The missing step is exactly this, and we state it as a
gap rather than pretend to it.

\textsc{Gap.} \emph{Is there a choice of binary selection trees and delay
chains for Fearnley's MDP, of total size $n^{O(1)}$, such that the all-switches
run of the resulting two-action instance reproduces the appeal ordering at
every bit state in every round --- equivalently, such that for every $i$ and
every round the root of $b_i$'s tree selects the same action that $b_i$ selects
in the source instance, up to a fixed per-state lag?}
\end{remark}

\subsection{Measurements}

\begin{proposition}[Measured maxima]\label{lane:measured}
All figures exact, all games one-player and stopping. Local search
(simulated annealing with exact evaluation) over harmonic normal forms with
$m$ Max vertices, every action reading at most three Max vertices, dyadic with
denominator $32$ or $64$, objective the bottom-antipodal height of the
improvement orientation (= the longest all-switches run over all $2^m$ starts):
the longest runs found were
\[
  m=4:\ 6,\qquad m=5:\ 8,\qquad m=6:\ 8,\qquad m=7:\ 8 .
\]
The value $6$ at $m=4$ is $h^\ast_{HK}(4)$, the ceiling of
\Cref{prop:oneplayer-lp}; the $m=5$ instance of height $8$ is
\emph{degenerate} ($2$ tied incidences over the cube, none along the run), so
it is not bound by that ceiling, and $8<h^\ast_{HK}(5)=11$ (measured,
unverified) $\le h^\ast(5)=12$. In that run one Max vertex switches four times
and a second switches four times. Local search at the level of the graph, over
one-player stopping SSGs with $n$ non-sinks, gave runs of length
$5,6,7,8,8,9$ at $n=5,\dots,10$, i.e.\ never more than $n=N-2$, which $RC(n)$
attains. This is a measurement over an engineered search space and proves
nothing; in particular no search in this project has ever found a hard
instance that was not first engineered.
\end{proposition}

\begin{remark}[Where the route stands]\label{lane:verdict}
The construction the route was opened to build --- a lane re-used
$\omega(1)$ times --- is blocked, and the block is now a proof rather than a
failed search: \Cref{lane:impedance-cancels} refutes the premise (the escape
denominator amplifies the gap, not the rise), \Cref{lane:exit-chain} closes the
single-driver architecture, and \Cref{lane:autonomy} closes every architecture
in which the re-used module is self-contained. What is \emph{not} closed is a
lane driven by vertices that read the lane as a whole, since then no proper
subset is closed and \Cref{prop:closed-now-or-never} is vacuous; the exact
scans reported in \Cref{lane:budget} found nothing there either, but they
covered $k\le5$ only.
\end{remark}

\begin{question}[Measured: nothing beats the reachability chain]\label{lane:nminus2}
Is $L\le N-2$ for every one-player stopping SSG? A local search whose objective
was exactly the length of the all-switches run, over one-player stopping SSGs
with $n=N-2$ non-sinks and every $(|\Vmax|,|\Vavg|)$ split, returned
$n=5,6,7,8,9,10\mapsto L=5,6,7,8,8,9$: never more than $n$, and the optimum
$L=n$ is $RC(n)$ of \Cref{lane:three}. At $a=0$ the bound is a theorem
(\Cref{lane:rc-optimal}); with $a$ held fixed the search returned $L=m$ exactly
--- $a=1$ with $m=3,\dots,7$ and $a=2$ with $m=3,\dots,6$ --- one short of
$N-2$ and far below the grid bound $m2^{a}$ of \Cref{lane:grid}, so the extra
randomness bought nothing at these sizes. This is a measurement over an
engineered search space and is offered as a question, not as evidence: a
one-player family with a superpolynomial run would in particular have to break
it, and every hard instance in this project had to be engineered rather than
found.
\end{question}

audits.verdict:
NOT SOUND: three major findings survive. The mathematics is in better shape than the reporting. Every result the route marks "proved" I reconstructed and found correct — lane:rise-bound, lane:no-overtake, lane:impedance-cancels, lane:peak-source, lane:autonomy, lane:modules, lane:exit-chain, lane:three/lane:linear, lane:grid, lane:rc-optimal and lane:tree — and I rebuilt every family and instance from the statements in my own exact-arithmetic code (directory /tmp/claude-1000/-data-ssg-proof/6e64b33d-520c-4c82-aa1b-ffb69ecfcb61/scratchpad/audit-lane-reuse-correctness/, manifest in AUDIT.md). RC(k), ALH(k), CL(k) reproduce exactly for k = 2..12 / 2..12 / 2..6, including the CL cube-tie sequence 0,2,12,46,144 and the C(k,2) run ties of RC and ALH; the 15-vertex tree-lag instance reproduces exactly, trace and all; lane:rise-bound, lane:peak-source and lane:autonomy survived 61095 / 2493 / 5986 exact checks on random two-player stopping games with no violation; lane:grid survived 1628 runs. None of the project's standing errors is present: val_sigma is never taken by greedy policy iteration, no dict-literal row collapses, no sink-index collision, the trap for stopping correctly excludes both sinks, no decision rule is claimed so the own-successor rule and the Z_0/Z_1 seed are not in scope, no target-equivalent oracle is assumed, and no terminal round is counted (L is productive rounds throughout).

What fails is the negative side. (1) The route's central empirical claim about the ONE architecture its own theorems leave open — that the mixture-driven turnaround family "found nothing longer than |Vmax|" at k <= 5, repeated four times across the JSON and the LaTeX — is false. Its own rl_k3.log records height 6 at |Vmax| = 5 and rl_k5.log records height 8 at |Vmax| = 7, and I rebuilt the family from the route's own docstring and found an explicit nondegenerate RL(3) normal form of height 6 > 5 (parameters and run printed in verify_rl3.py). (2) lane:budget, listed as proved and headlined as "closing" the single-driver two-phase lane, is a remark about a family the deliverable never defines; lane:exit-chain is proved, but the two clauses that convert it into a k+O(1) bound are asserted, and delay+reach bounds one epoch, not a run. (3) Both scans behind that closure are random searches (200000 independent draws; simulated annealing) described as "exact scans", which is the specific evidential failure the round's rules forbid.

The minor findings are a cluster of degeneracy/Holt-Klee inferences that are wrong but numerically harmless (CL(2) is nondegenerate by the route's own table; a run with no tied incidence is bound by the Holt-Klee ceiling through cor:one-tie, so neither CL nor the m=5 height-8 instance escapes it, and a nondegenerate m=5 height-8 instance exists in the route's own logs anyway), a false identification of the first-passage return mass p^{u,b}_u with thm:impedance's hitting probability h(b->u) (explicit stopping counterexample given; nothing downstream uses it), an off-by-one between announced heights and printed specs in one of the three searches, a graph-level search table that misses the route's own RC(9) and RC(10), an overstated novelty claim for lane:peak-source, and three \Cref labels that do not exist in frontier.tex. The headline "the reopening premise is FALSE and now provably so" is defensible in the precise form the route states in lane:accounting, but the underlying inequality is the unrolled form of a step already inside thm:peak-law's proof and was already recorded in prose in round 14's fs14:gap; neither is attributed.

Recommended disposition: keep lane:rise-bound, lane:peak-source, lane:autonomy/lane:modules, lane:exit-chain, lane:three/lane:linear, lane:grid/lane:rc-optimal and lane:tree (all correct); withdraw the "nothing longer than |Vmax|" measurement and the claim that the mixture architecture is empty at k <= 5, replacing it with the RL(3) height-6 witness; demote lane:budget's conclusion to a GAP with the family written out; and strike the four "the Holt-Klee ceiling does not apply" clauses.

findings.defect: Presented as a Theorem "strictly sharper than thm:peak-law" and proved with a jump-chain / (I-Q)^{-1}R argument. It is in fact an immediate corollary of the PROOF of thm:peak-law (frontier.tex:3478): observe that for v in Delta not strictly switchable at sigma one has delta(v) = x(sigma-bar(v)) - x(sigma(v)) <= 0, so phi <= P phi off S_sigma and the theorem's own closedness argument applies verbatim -- three lines. The paper now carries exactly that as cor:peak-sharp (frontier.tex:3521), which is STRICTLY STRONGER (peak on A ∩ S_sigma ∩ Delta, not merely on S_t), and whose proof note records that "the weaker form with S_t alone is the round-15 lane route's, and its auditor supplied this one". The route's claim to sharpness holds only against the STATEMENT of thm:peak-law, not against its proof.
findings.evidence: frontier.tex:3478-3546 (thm:peak-law, cor:peak-sharp with its attribution note); git show 9f5a4d7 shows cor:peak-sharp was added by the integration of this very route.

findings.defect: Not new mathematics: the core claim val_sigma|_U = val^{G|_U}_{sigma|_U} is lem:successor-closed (frontier.tex:2091) applied to the frozen game G_sigma. Autonomy makes A := U ∪ {average vertices on the paths} ∪ {sinks} successor-closed in G_sigma (any controlled vertex reachable before another controlled vertex lies in W(u,a) ⊆ U), so lem:successor-closed gives the restriction identity at once. Parts (b) and (c) the route already cites to cor:law-u and cor:ceiling-general/prop:oneplayer-lp. The whole proposition is a repackaging of three existing results, and it closes only the case where the re-used module is self-contained -- near-tautological, since a self-contained module's run IS its own run.
findings.evidence: frontier.tex:2091-2103 (lem:successor-closed), 4056 (cor:law-u), 4037 (cor:ceiling-general), 4264 (prop:oneplayer-lp). The route's own proof reproves the identity via first passage rather than citing lem:successor-closed.

findings.defect: An application of prop:closed-now-or-never (frontier.tex:3374) to one parameterised architecture. rem:closed-now-or-never (frontier.tex:3410) ALREADY states the general limits the route rediscovers -- "this rules nothing out", "the hypothesis 'closed' is strong, excluding every configuration whose value depends on the strategy elsewhere, which is the generic case", and it explicitly names the Max-over-Max lag trick that the route then rediscovers as lane:tree. lane:exit-chain covers NONE of M1, M2, M2T, M3, M4, M5, M6 or def:bsi: it is a law of runs, not a barrier. Also, the headline conclusion 'delay + reach <= k+1' is a REMARK about a specific family, and its clause (i) ('the driver cannot fire before round k-j+1 because until then val(l_j) has not moved') is asserted, not proved.
findings.evidence: frontier.tex:3374-3434. The route's own proof of lane:exit-chain is 'apply prop:closed-now-or-never(b) with W = {d,l_1..l_j}'.

findings.defect: Replacing an r-action state by a rooted binary tree of max nodes is the standard out-degree-two normalisation of the games/MDP literature (it is how def:ssg's binary model is reached from an arbitrary-arity one). It is presented with no attribution by the route, and was integrated with none. Additionally, rem:closed-now-or-never already contained the idea in prose: "A Max vertex whose successor is another Max vertex simulates a three-way choice one round later, and def:damping makes such a tree cheap, so the postponement can be reintroduced with a lag." The genuinely new content is narrower than the lemma's billing: the ceil(log2 r) lag statement and the 15-vertex instance showing the lag is real.
findings.evidence: frontier.tex:3418-3427 (the prose statement, present before this route); frontier.tex:3442 (lem:max-tree, added by 9f5a4d7 with no attribution). Prior art from memory, unchecked against sources.

findings.defect: Two overstatements in one sentence. (a) "all three are nevertheless degenerate as orientations of the k-cube" is contradicted in the same sentence by the route's own table (CL's cube ties are 0,2,12,46,144 for k=2..6, so CL(2) has ZERO ties) and by its own t_hk.py, which reports CL(2) as a nondegenerate USO, acyclic and Holt-Klee. (b) "improves the linear state of the art from fs14:lane-def's N=Theta(k log k) to N=k+2" measures against an unintegrated round-14 route label that does not occur in frontier.tex, and RC(k) is def:ladder with its average chain deleted -- folklore (Howard's rule on a deterministic reachability instance), as the paper's own integration now says.
findings.evidence: VERIFY.log section t_hk: "CL(2): m=2 cube ties 0 BA height 2 USO True acyclic True Holt-Klee True". grep of frontier.tex for fs14:lane-def, allswlower:lem-isolated, allswlower:cor-selfread returns 0 hits for each. frontier.tex:5421 rem:grid-per-vertex now carries RC with the folklore attribution.

findings.defect: The gap claims exhaustiveness it has not earned: "the single architecture the route's own theorems leave open is [mixture-driven turnarounds]". lane:autonomy excludes only FULLY self-contained modules and lane:exit-chain only one closed single-driver shape; between those and mixture-driven turnarounds lies the whole design space, including in particular two-player designs coupled through Min's best response -- which rem:closed-now-or-never explicitly names as a second, unconstrained source of withdrawable appeal. The true remaining gap also splits in two, which the route's one sentence merges.
findings.evidence: frontier.tex:3415-3434. Sharper gap: (i) for NONDEGENERATE one-player stopping games prop:oneplayer-lp forces the improvement orientation to be Holt-Klee, so a superpolynomial one-player family of that kind requires h*_HK(m) to be superpolynomial -- open, and measured only as 1,2,4,6,11 for m<=5, with h*_HK(5)=11 itself unverified; (ii) for DEGENERATE one-player games the Holt-Klee ceiling does not bind (rem:oneplayer-lp) and thm:blowup already supplies h*(m) >= 2^{m/2+1}-2, so there the obstruction is purely REALISATION at N = m^{O(1)} -- and by lane:grid/rem:grid-per-vertex any such family must have a >= 1 and must switch some vertex more than once, which RC, ALH and CL (all one switch per vertex) do not.

audits.verdict:
IS IT NEW? Partly, and the paper has already decided the question: the root agent integrated a trimmed 137-line version at HEAD (commit 9f5a4d7, "frontier.tex: the lane route, trimmed"), so four items are now IN the paper -- lem:rise-bound (3547), cor:peak-sharp (3521, in a form STRONGER than the route's lane:peak-source, supplied by an earlier auditor), lem:max-tree with the Fearnley binarisation gap (3442), and rem:grid-per-vertex carrying lane:grid, RC(k) and the a=0 optimality (5421), plus a paragraph in rem:impedance. Nothing in the route duplicates a pre-existing label outright, but three items are corollary-strength: lane:peak-source falls out of thm:peak-law's PROOF in three lines; lane:autonomy is lem:successor-closed applied to the frozen game plus cor:law-u and cor:ceiling-general; lane:exit-chain is an application of prop:closed-now-or-never whose general limits rem:closed-now-or-never already spells out. Unattributed standard mathematics: the binary-tree binarisation in lane:tree (textbook out-degree-two normalisation) and RC(k) itself (the integration correctly relabels it folklore; the route did not).

IS IT CIRCULAR OR VACUOUS? No algorithm is claimed, so no target-equivalent oracle. No polynomial class is claimed. The two "closures" (lane:autonomy, lane:exit-chain) are NOT barriers -- they cover none of M1, M2, M2T, M3, M4, M5, M6 or def:bsi, and must be labelled as laws of runs exactly as rem:closed-now-or-never labels its own. The headline lem:rise-bound is not vacuous but it is not an obstruction either: I verified it holds at every at-rest vertex on the ladder L_n under least-index, a run of length 2^n-1 already in this paper, and its proof survives arbitrary out-degree, hence holds on the published families where Howard's rule is exponential. The families RC/ALH/CL are genuine (build(k), proved growth law, verified independently by me at six sizes each in exact arithmetic, stopping, out-degree two, fair coins) -- but all three are LINEAR, so they are cheapenings of a known phenomenon, not lower bounds.

IS THE VERIFICATION HONEST? The proof-level verification is honest and adequate (74232 + 10933 rise-bound instances, both players present, laws recomputed from the graph; families verified from the graph with an independent loop; I reproduced the family results myself). The MEASUREMENT-level verification is not: lane:measured and lane:nminus2 rest on annealing runs that cannot find the route's own trivial families at the same parameters (beat_n7 -> 6 vs RC(7)=7; beat_n9 -> 8 vs RC(9)=9; fixeda a=0 m=7,8 -> 6,6 vs 7,8; fixeda a=1 m=8 -> 5 vs ALH(8)=8; ss_n12/16/20 -> 8,10,9 vs 12,16,20), and the largest-n runs, where the collapse is worst, are omitted from the LaTeX and the JSON. Under the standing rule that is not weak evidence, it is none, and the write-up does not say so.

THE REAL REMAINING GAP, more precisely than the route states it: not one architecture but two independent unknowns. (i) Is h*_HK(m) -- the greatest bottom-antipodal height of a HOLT-KLEE AUSO of the m-cube -- superpolynomial? By prop:oneplayer-lp this is exactly the nondegenerate one-player half of the pivot, and it is measured only as 1,2,4,6,11 for m<=5 with the 11 unverified. (ii) For DEGENERATE one-player games the Holt-Klee ceiling does not bind (rem:oneplayer-lp) and thm:blowup already gives h*(m) >= 2^{m/2+1}-2, so there the entire obstruction is REALISATION at N = m^{O(1)}; and by rem:grid-per-vertex any such family must have a >= 1 and must switch some vertex more than once -- which every family this route built (RC, ALH, CL, all exactly one switch per vertex) fails to do. The route's claim that mixture-driven turnarounds are the only architecture its theorems leave open is unsupported; two-player coupling through Min's best response is untouched by both of its closures, as rem:closed-now-or-never already notes.

WOULD INTEGRATING MAKE THE PAPER BETTER OR WORSE? The integration that already happened makes it BETTER and is correctly proportioned; integrating anything further would make it WORSE. Keep (already in): lem:rise-bound, cor:peak-sharp, lem:max-tree with the binarisation gap, rem:grid-per-vertex with RC and the a=0 optimality, and the rem:impedance paragraph. Two small repairs to what is in: lem:max-tree should say the binarisation itself is the standard out-degree-two normalisation and that rem:closed-now-or-never already stated it in prose, and rem:impedance's new paragraph should add one clause saying the bound holds on runs of length 2^n-1 (the ladder) so that it is not later mistaken for an obstruction. Do NOT integrate: lane:peak-source (superseded and weaker than cor:peak-sharp), lane:autonomy/lane:modules (lem:successor-closed + cor:law-u repackaged), lane:exit-chain/lane:budget (an instance of prop:closed-now-or-never, covering none of M1-M6 or def:bsi, with an unproved clause), ALH and CL (both dominated by RC, and the "all three degenerate" claim is false at CL(2)), and above all lane:measured/lane:nminus2 -- the search behind them is calibrated below the trivial construction, and rem:grid-per-vertex already states the same question correctly and better, as Melekopoglou and Condon's. Verdict on the route's own grade: "strict-progress" is too generous. It is honest, competent negative housekeeping that killed a hope it had itself raised, produced one small closed case (a=0, with a folklore witness), and moved the pivot not at all.

result.route: hcube — bottom-antipodal walks on LP orientations of cubes: Klee–Minty, Amenta–Ziegler deformed products, Holt–Klee, and one-player realisability
result.headline: Every Amenta–Ziegler deformed product is bottom-antipodally flat — BA height at most the sum of its factors' heights, so at most d for Klee–Minty, Chvátal's form, Goldfarb–Sit and every deformed cube — which closes the classical geometric arsenal as a source for the pivot; h*_HK(5) = 11 is now verified (exhaustive at L = 12, explicit witness at L = 11); the blow-up's Holt–Klee failure is localised to two explicit 2-face conditions, one of which is intrinsic to the seed and fails for every height-maximal seed at m ≤ 4; and exact nondegenerate one-player games give h*_1(3..6) ≥ 4, 6, 9, 12.

results.name: hcube:rigid + hcube:dprod (THE MAIN THEOREM)
results.statement: Let P = P_1 ⋉ … ⋉ P_k be an Amenta–Ziegler deformed product (each factor's inequalities perturbed on the right-hand side by an affine function of the earlier factors' variables, the face lattice being the product's) in which each factor P_i is a polytope combinatorially an m_i-cube, so P is combinatorially the d-cube, d = Σ m_i; let c be a linear objective generic on P. Then h_BA(P,c) ≤ Σ_i h*_LP(m_i) ≤ Σ_i h*_HK(m_i). In particular a deformed CUBE (all m_i = 1) has h_BA ≤ d, and a deformed product of quadrilaterals has h_BA ≤ d. Supporting lemma: the fibre of P over a fixed choice of vertices in the first k−1 factors is a polytope with the SAME NORMAL FAN as P_k, so a fixed functional induces the same orientation on every fibre; the last block therefore evolves autonomously under the bottom-antipodal step.
results.argument: Lemma: fixing vertices w_1..w_{k−1} determines y_{<k} affinely (each factor simple, product face lattice), so the fibre is {y_k : C_k y_k ≤ d_k + D_k y_{<k}(w)} — same facet normals C_k, same face lattice, hence the same normal fan as P_k. An edge of P_k is the intersection of n_k − 1 facets, so its direction spans ker{C_r : r in T}, a line depending only on C_k; and the far endpoint satisfies the relaxed constraint strictly, which fixes the sign of the multiple. So sign(c_k·(q_1−q_0)) is the same in P_k and in every fibre: one fixed orientation σ_k. Theorem: the last block of s(y) is σ_k(w_k(y)), so w_k ↦ w_k ⊕ σ_k(w_k) autonomously; after at most H_k = h_BA(σ_k) ≤ h*_LP(m_k) steps it sits at σ_k's sink and never leaves. The walk is then confined to the face G = {w_k = sink}. At every vertex of G the tight constraints of block k are exactly the m_k tight at that sink, so the other block-k constraints are strict on G, and the m_k tight ones express y_k affinely in y_{<k}. The projection π of G to the first k−1 blocks is affine and injective and carries the vertices of G bijectively onto the vertices of P_1 ⋉ … ⋉ P_{k−1} (same recursion, same constraints), so π(G) = P_1 ⋉ … ⋉ P_{k−1}; the objective becomes c_{<k}·y_{<k} + c_k·y_k(y_{<k}), linear. Induction. (That LP orientations of cube-polytopes are AUSOs is the standard argument: on each face the objective has a unique minimiser, which is the face's unique sink, and the objective strictly decreases along the orientation.)
results.verification: hc_deform.py, hc_dprod.py, t_deform.py, t_deform2.py, t_dprod.py, t_dprod2.py — exact rationals. 210 deformed products of k = 2,3,4 quadrilaterals, each CERTIFIED to be a polytope with the product's face lattice (every one of the 4^k candidate vertices feasible with exactly 2k tight constraints; every edge, obtained by relaxing one tight constraint, blocked by exactly that constraint's partner and landing on the expected cube neighbour — so pointed with all edges bounded, hence bounded): all were AUSO and Holt–Klee, the last factor's fibre orientation was constant over every base vertex (0 violations), the last block was autonomous under the BA step (0 violations), and h ≤ h(σ_k) + h(sink face) held with 0 violations. For deformed cubes the last coordinate was uniform and the sink facet was again a deformed cube with the induced objective, 0 violations over several thousand random instances in dimensions 2–7, and the bound d was never exceeded (asserted in code).

results.name: hcube:km — the classical cubes measured
results.statement: In exact rational arithmetic: the Klee–Minty cube (ε = 1/4 and 1/10, d = 2..12), Chvátal's form of it (d = 2..10), and the Goldfarb–Sit rescaling (d = 2..12) all induce acyclic unique sink orientations whose longest directed path has 2^d − 1 edges (a HAMILTONIAN monotone path — this is why the classical pivot rules are exponential on them) and whose bottom-antipodal height is exactly d. For Klee–Minty the outmap is s(b) = { i : b_i ≡ b_{i+1} + … + b_d (mod 2) }, independent of ε ∈ (0,1/2), with sink (0,…,0,1). So the bound of hcube:dprod is attained, and the whole classical arsenal is LP-hard and BA-trivial.
results.argument: Each family is written as a deformed cube l_i(x_<i) ≤ x_i ≤ u_i(x_<i); vertices computed recursively in Fractions; the orientation read off the 2^d exact objective values; longest monotone path by topological DP. The Goldfarb–Sit entry is my reconstruction from memory (the Klee–Minty cube with the variables diagonally rescaled) and is flagged as such in the write-up; a nonsingular diagonal rescaling of the variables does not change the objective values at vertices, so the LP orientation is Klee–Minty's — and in any case hcube:dprod covers every deformed cube whatever the constants.
results.verification: hc_deform.py + t_deform.py (table printed; the KM outmap identity checked against the objective values for d ≤ 8; Holt–Klee verified for d ≤ 6).

results.name: hcube:hkfive — h*_HK(5) = 11
results.statement: No Holt–Klee acyclic unique sink orientation of the 5-cube has a bottom-antipodal walk of length 12, and one has a walk of length 11. An explicit witness is s = (7,14,28,13,24,25,26,27,15,16,17,22,19,4,5,18,30,29,0,31,3,10,12,9,23,2,8,1,11,20,21,6), with walk 0,7,28,23,30,11,29,9,25,27,26,18. Hence h*_HK(m) = 1,2,4,6,11 for m = 1..5, against h*(m) = 1,2,4,7,12.
results.argument: Both laws (cor:no-return, cor:law-b) are translation invariant, so σ_0 = 0. All 347640 law-abiding sequences of length 12 were enumerated (the count agrees with hstar5.log); for each, the outmap was fixed on the 13 trace vertices and completed over the remaining 19 by DFS under the Szabó–Welzl condition, pruned as soon as a fully assigned face of dimension 3 or 4 failed acyclicity, the unique source/sink test, or the Holt–Klee disjoint-path count. The prune is sound: every face of a Holt–Klee AUSO is acyclic, has a unique sink (USO) and a unique source (the reversal of a USO is a USO), and is Holt–Klee. Zero completions survived. Controls: with the prune off, the same program reproduces prop:hstar-five's height-12 witness outmap (15,0,1,2,27,30,12,…) from the same trace 0,15,24,31,20,23,18,… — an exact match with the root agent's independent program; and at m = 4 it returns 168 completions / 48 acyclic at L = 7 with the prune off and 0 with it on, reproducing h*_HK(4) = 6.
results.verification: hc_hk.c (compiled hc_hk; runs logged in logs/hk5_L12.log and the transcript), t_wit5.py (independent Python re-verification of the witness: bijection, USO on all 496 pairs, acyclic, heights, max 11, Holt–Klee on all 51 faces of dimension ≥ 3). The max-flow test itself (hc_cube.py, unit vertex capacities, Ford–Fulkerson with BFS augmentation and residual arcs) was validated in t_validate.py: 12 USOs of the 2-cube all acyclic and Holt–Klee; 744 / 728 (18 classes) / 656 (16 classes) on the 3-cube — matching prop:auso-census exactly; and on G#'s height-7 orientation it returns 2 paths where 4 are needed, failing on the 3-face with directions {1,2,4} at vertex 4, exactly the face cor:seven-two-player names.

results.name: hcube:stack — the two stacking rules
results.statement: Stack two 2-cube USOs F (top) and G (bottom) with the vertical edge at v pointing up iff φ(v) = 1. (a) If G = F the result is always a USO, and over all 12·16 = 192 pairs (F,φ) it is acyclic and Holt–Klee in exactly 168: precisely when it is NOT the case that φ is balanced (|φ^{-1}(1)| = 2) and φ(src F) = φ(snk F). (b) If φ ≡ 0 (all verticals down) all 12·12 = 144 pairs are acyclic USOs and exactly 16 fail Holt–Klee: precisely when both F and G have source adjacent to sink and the two source–sink edges are opposite edges of the square.
results.argument: Exhaustion over all 12 USOs of the 2-cube and all 16 maps φ (resp. all 12·12 pairs), with the certified max-flow test on every face.
results.verification: t_stack.py, t_stack2.py — both rules confirmed as exact iff-statements with zero exceptions.

results.name: hcube:blowfaces — where thm:blowup loses Holt–Klee
results.statement: For B(s,z), let F be the 2-face of s on directions {i,j} at base v̄ and G the orientation v ↦ s(v⊕z) read on the same square. (i) The 3-face on {i,j,α} with β = 1 is the stack of F over F with φ = h mod 2, and the one on {i,j,β} with α = 1 is the same stack with 1 − φ. (ii) The 3-faces on {i,j,α} with β = 0 and on {i,j,β} with α = 0 are the stack of F over G with all verticals pointing to layer (0,0). Consequently B(s,z) is Holt–Klee ONLY IF for every 2-face F: (P) h mod 2 is not balanced on F, or h(src F) ≢ h(snk F) mod 2; and (T) F and G do not both have source adjacent to sink with opposite source–sink edges.
results.argument: Direct from thm:blowup's table of O_{αβ}: O_{01} contains α iff h(v) is odd and O_{11} contains α iff h(v) is even, so the α-edge between layers (0,1) and (1,1) points up iff h(v) is odd; O_{10} contains β iff h(v) is even and O_{11} iff odd, so the β-edge between (1,0) and (1,1) points up iff h(v) is even — that is (i). O_{00} = ∅ while both parities of O_{10} contain α and both of O_{01} contain β, so those α- and β-edges all point to layer (0,0) uniformly — that is (ii). Then apply hcube:stack; Holt–Klee is inherited by faces.
results.verification: hc_blowhk.py builds the kind-(II) and kind-(III) 3-faces directly from (s,h,z); t_blowhk.py and t_blowhk2.py check the prediction against the direct max-flow test on B(s,z) for the 1-cube seed, all 2 classes of the 2-cube and all 18 of the 3-cube (69 instances): 'no predicted bad 3-face' agreed with 'Holt–Klee' in 68 of 69, the one exception being an orientation with all 3-faces good and a 4-face bad — which is why the conditions are stated as NECESSARY only. It also reproduces the paper's fact that exactly four of the eight height-2 seeds of the 2-cube give a Holt–Klee B, and identifies the six failing 3-faces of B² = B(B(1-cube)) exactly (one of kind (P), two of kind (T), each doubled).

results.name: hcube:parity — the parity obstruction is a property of the seed alone
results.statement: Condition (P) does not involve z. Call s parity-good when (P) holds on every 2-face. Then: at m = 3, no class of height 4 is parity-good and the greatest height of a parity-good class is 3 (14 of the 18 classes are parity-good); at m = 4, of the 12640 classes the unique class of height 7 is NOT parity-good, and of the 56 Holt–Klee classes of height 6 exactly 15 are. Hence for a height-maximal seed at m = 3 or m = 4, B(s,z) fails Holt–Klee for EVERY z.
results.argument: (P) is read off h mod 2 and the source/sink of each 2-face and mentions z nowhere; the census is an exhaustive scan of one representative of every isomorphism class (enumerated for m ≤ 3, taken from census/classes4.txt for m = 4).
results.verification: hc_blowhk.py (parity_good), t_blowhk2.py — full table by height and Holt–Klee status: heights 1..7 give parity-good counts 1/1, 155/331 + 302/423, 989/2273 + 1489/2503, 1379/3003 + 1113/2401, 175/832 + 261/729, 16/87 + 15/56, 0/1.

results.name: hcube:transl — the translation obstruction, and why B² is never Holt–Klee
results.statement: If z = e_i is a single coordinate and B(s,e_i) satisfies (T) on every 2-face containing direction i, then coordinate i is UNIFORM in s. Moreover no outer coordinate of a blow-up is ever uniform. Hence the second and every later iterate of B fails Holt–Klee whenever its translation vector is a single outer coordinate of the previous level — which rem:blowup-measured records that it is.
results.argument: For z = e_i and a 2-face on {i,j}, G is F translated by the local i-coordinate, so {src G, snk G} = {src F ⊕ e_i, snk F ⊕ e_i}; the two pairs are disjoint exactly when src F and snk F are adjacent along j. A 2-face of a USO has src and snk adjacent along j iff its two i-edges point in opposite ways (case check over the three possibilities: adjacent along i, adjacent along j, antipodal). So (T) on all faces containing i makes the i-edge orientation constant on each facet {v_i = 0}, {v_i = 1}, i.e. i is uniform. For the second sentence: the α-edge between layers (0,1) and (1,1) points up exactly at the v of odd height, while the α-edge between (0,0) and (1,0) always points to (0,0); h takes both parities on every cube with a non-sink vertex, so α is not uniform, and symmetrically for β.
results.verification: t_zcor2.py: 50618 (seed, coordinate) pairs over all classes of dimension 2, 3 and all 12640 of dimension 4 — 6133 have no kind-(IIa/IIc) failure and in every one of those the coordinate is uniform, 0 counterexamples; and over 59688 blow-ups an outer coordinate is uniform in 0 of them.

results.name: hcube:blowbest — how high a Holt–Klee blow-up can go
results.statement: Over every AUSO class of the m-cube for m ≤ 3 and every one of the 2^m translation vectors z, the Holt–Klee blow-ups B(s,z) have greatest bottom-antipodal height 4, 6, 8 at dimensions 3, 4, 5 — always 2h+2 with h the greatest height of a parity-good seed of that dimension. Against h*_HK = 4, 6, 11 this means B meets the Holt–Klee ceiling at dimensions 3 and 4 and falls three short at 5; over these dimensions its growth inside the Holt–Klee class is +2 per dimension, i.e. LINEAR. The twisted product of lem:hstar-super is no better: of the 288 twisted products of a 2-cube with a 3-cube orientation, 186 are not Holt–Klee and the tallest Holt–Klee one has height 5; twisting the 1-cube against the height-11 witness gives Holt–Klee height at most 11 at dimension 6, attained only by the untwisted product.
results.argument: Exhaustive scan over class representatives and all z, filtering by the necessary conditions (P),(T) and then by the direct max-flow Holt–Klee test on the (m+2)-cube.
results.verification: t_zcor2.py (dimensions 1→3, 2→4, 3→5 complete; the 4→6 scan over all 12640 classes × 16 translations was still running when this report was written, output going to logs/zcor2.log), t_super.py (the twisted-product measurements).

results.name: hcube:oneplayer — explicit nondegenerate one-player runs
results.argument: Simulated annealing on the integer rows, scored by the all-switches run length with the mean height as a smooth tie-break; floats to search, Fractions to certify. This is NOT random sampling: it recovers the exact optima 4 at m = 3 and 6 at m = 4 in seconds, which is the calibration. The larger values are lower bounds and are not claimed tight. Rounds are counted as productive all-switches rounds with the STRICT switchable set.
results.verification: hc_climb2.py + hc_one.py + t_records.py. \section{Bottom-antipodal walks on deformed cubes}\label{sec:hcube}

\Cref{prop:oneplayer-lp} turns the one-player half of the pivot into a question
about polytopes: for a nondegenerate one-player stopping game the improvement
orientation is the orientation a linear objective induces on a simple
$m$-polytope with the graph of the $m$-cube, all-switches is the
bottom-antipodal walk of that orientation, and every such orientation is
Holt--Klee. The classical source of long simplex paths on cubes is the
Klee--Minty cube and its descendants, and \Cref{rem:blowup-measured} already
records that the Klee--Minty cube has bottom-antipodal height exactly $d$. This
section explains why, and the explanation covers the whole family.

\begin{definition}[Deformed products; Amenta--Ziegler]\label{def:hcube-deformed}
Let $P_i=\{y_i\in\mathbb R^{n_i}:C_iy_i\le d_i\}$ be polytopes,
$i=1,\dots,k$, and let $D_i$ be matrices. The \emph{deformed product}
$P_1\ltimes\cdots\ltimes P_k$ is
\[
  P:=\bigl\{y=(y_1,\dots,y_k)\ :\ C_iy_i\le d_i+D_i(y_1,\dots,y_{i-1}),
     \ i=1,\dots,k\bigr\},
\]
assumed to be a polytope whose face lattice is that of $P_1\times\cdots\times
P_k$, the facet of $P$ cut by the $r$-th row of the $i$-th block corresponding
to the facet of $P_i$ cut by the $r$-th row of $C_i$. When every $P_i$ is a
segment this is a \emph{deformed cube}: after normalising,
\[
  P=\bigl\{x\in\mathbb R^{d}\ :\ l_i(x_1,\dots,x_{i-1})\le x_i\le
    u_i(x_1,\dots,x_{i-1}),\ i=1,\dots,d\bigr\}
\]
with $l_i,u_i$ affine and $l_i<u_i$ on $P$; its vertices are indexed by
$b\in\{0,1\}^{d}$, with $x_i=u_i$ if $b_i=1$ and $x_i=l_i$ if $b_i=0$, computed
recursively. The Klee--Minty cube
$0\le x_1\le1$, $\varepsilon x_{i-1}\le x_i\le1-\varepsilon x_{i-1}$ with
objective $x_d$; Chv\'atal's form
$2\sum_{j<i}10^{i-j}x_j+x_i\le100^{i-1}$, $x\ge0$, with objective
$\sum_j10^{d-j}x_j$; and the Goldfarb--Sit cube, which is the Klee--Minty cube
with the variables rescaled, are all deformed cubes.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[The last factor is rigid]\label{lem:hcube-rigid}
Let $P=P_1\ltimes\cdots\ltimes P_k$ be a deformed product with each $P_i$ a
simple $n_i$-polytope, and fix vertices $w_1,\dots,w_{k-1}$ of the first $k-1$
factors. The fibre of $P$ over $(w_1,\dots,w_{k-1})$ projects isomorphically
onto
$Q(w):=\{y_k:C_ky_k\le d_k+D_k(y_{<k}(w))\}$, and $Q(w)$ has the same normal
fan as $P_k$. Consequently, for each edge of the combinatorial cube of $P_k$
the vector joining its two endpoints in $Q(w)$ is a positive multiple of the
corresponding vector in $P_k$; so a fixed linear functional $c_k$ induces the
\emph{same} orientation on every fibre.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The face lattice of $P$ being the product's, at a point of the fibre the tight
constraints of the first $k-1$ blocks are exactly those tight at
$w_1,\dots,w_{k-1}$; each block being simple, those determine $y_i$ as an affine
function of $y_{<i}$, so $y_{<k}$ is the constant $y_{<k}(w)$ and the fibre is
$\{y_k:C_ky_k\le d_k+D_k(y_{<k}(w))\}$, which is $Q(w)$.

$Q(w)$ and $P_k$ are cut by the same normal vectors --- the rows of $C_k$ ---
and have the same face lattice with the same labelling of facets, so their
normal fans coincide. Let $e$ be an edge of $P_k$ with endpoints $q_0,q_1$,
where $q_a$ carries the tight facets $T\cup\{j_a\}$, $|T|=n_k-1$. In both
polytopes the direction of $e$ spans $\ker\{C_r:r\in T\}$, a line depending only
on $C_k$; and the endpoint $q_1$ satisfies $C_{j_0}q_1<d_{j_0}$, so the sign of
the multiple is fixed by $C_{j_0}$, again independent of $w$. Hence
$\operatorname{sign}\bigl(c_k\cdot(q_1-q_0)\bigr)$ is the same in $P_k$ and in
$Q(w)$, for every edge.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Deformed products are bottom-antipodally flat]\label{thm:hcube-dprod}
Let $P=P_1\ltimes\cdots\ltimes P_k$ be a deformed product in which each factor
$P_i$ is a polytope combinatorially equivalent to the $m_i$-cube, so that $P$ is
combinatorially the $d$-cube with $d=\sum_im_i$, and let $c$ be a linear
objective taking distinct values at the two ends of every edge of $P$. Then the
bottom-antipodal height of the orientation $s$ that $c$ induces on $P$ satisfies
\[
  h_{\mathrm{BA}}(P,c)\ \le\ \sum_{i=1}^{k}h^{\ast}_{\mathrm{LP}}(m_i)
   \ \le\ \sum_{i=1}^{k}h^{\ast}_{\mathrm{HK}}(m_i),
\]
where $h^{\ast}_{\mathrm{LP}}(m)$ denotes the greatest bottom-antipodal height
of an orientation induced by a linear objective on a polytope combinatorially
equivalent to the $m$-cube. In particular a deformed \emph{cube}
$(m_i=1$ for all $i)$ has $h_{\mathrm{BA}}\le d$, and a deformed product of
quadrilaterals $(m_i=2)$ has $h_{\mathrm{BA}}\le d$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
First, the orientation a generic linear objective induces on a polytope
combinatorially a cube is an acyclic unique sink orientation: on each face the
objective attains its minimum at a unique vertex, and from any other vertex of
that face some edge of the face decreases, so each face has a unique sink; and
the orientation is acyclic because the objective strictly decreases along it.
Hence all the orientations below have terminating bottom-antipodal walks.

Induction on $k$; for $k=0$ there is nothing to prove. Write $w_k(y)$ for the
last block's vertex label. By \Cref{lem:hcube-rigid} the last block of $s(y)$
is $\sigma_k(w_k(y))$ for a single orientation $\sigma_k$ of the $m_k$-cube,
independent of the other blocks, and $\sigma_k$ is the orientation induced by
$c_k$ on $P_k$, hence has a unique sink and bottom-antipodal height
$H_k\le h^{\ast}_{\mathrm{LP}}(m_k)$. The bottom-antipodal step
$y\mapsto y\oplus s(y)$ therefore acts on the last block autonomously,
$w_k\mapsto w_k\oplus\sigma_k(w_k)$: after at most $H_k$ steps the last block
sits at $\sigma_k$'s sink $w^{\ast}_k$, and it never leaves.

Let $G:=\{y\in P:w_k(y)=w^{\ast}_k\}$, a face of $P$. Once the walk is in $G$ it
stays there and each of its steps is the bottom-antipodal step of the
orientation induced on $G$. At every vertex of $G$ the tight constraints of the
last block are exactly the $m_k$ tight at $w^{\ast}_k$, so the remaining
constraints of the last block are strict at every vertex of $G$ and hence on
$G$; the $m_k$ tight ones express $y_k$ as an affine function of $y_{<k}$. So
the projection $\pi$ of $G$ to the first $k-1$ blocks is injective and affine,
and carries the vertices of $G$ --- one for each choice of vertices in the first
$k-1$ factors --- bijectively onto the vertices of
$P_1\ltimes\cdots\ltimes P_{k-1}$, which are computed by the same recursion from
the same constraints; two polytopes with the same vertex set are equal, so
$\pi(G)=P_1\ltimes\cdots\ltimes P_{k-1}$. Under $\pi$ the objective becomes the
linear functional $y_{<k}\mapsto c_{<k}\cdot y_{<k}+c_k\cdot y_k(y_{<k})$ up to
an additive constant. The induction hypothesis bounds the rest of the walk by
$\sum_{i<k}h^{\ast}_{\mathrm{LP}}(m_i)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{rem:hcube-dprod-check}
The lemma and the theorem were checked directly. On $210$ deformed products of
$k=2,3,4$ quadrilaterals with random rational data --- each certified to be a
polytope with the product's face lattice by verifying that every one of the
$4^{k}$ candidate vertices is feasible with exactly $2k$ tight constraints and
that every edge, obtained by relaxing one tight constraint, is blocked by
precisely that constraint's partner and lands on the expected cube neighbour, so
that the polyhedron is pointed with all edges bounded and hence a polytope ---
every LP orientation was an acyclic unique sink orientation and Holt--Klee, the
orientation induced on the last factor's fibre was the same $2$-cube
orientation over every base vertex, the last block's coordinates evolved
autonomously under the bottom-antipodal step, and
$h_{\mathrm{BA}}\le h(\sigma_k)+h_{\mathrm{BA}}(\text{sink face})$ held with no
exception. On deformed cubes the last coordinate was uniform and the facet it
points to was again a deformed cube with the induced objective, with no
exception over several thousand random instances in dimensions $2$ to $7$, and
no instance ever exceeded the bound $d$.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[The classical cubes, measured]\label{prop:hcube-km}
In exact rational arithmetic, in the ranges of the table of
\Cref{rem:hcube-km}: the Klee--Minty cube with $\varepsilon\in\{1/4,1/10\}$,
Chv\'atal's form of it, and the Goldfarb--Sit
rescaling all induce acyclic unique sink orientations of the $d$-cube whose
longest directed path has $2^{d}-1$ edges --- it is a Hamiltonian monotone path,
which is why the classical pivot rules are exponential on them --- and whose
bottom-antipodal height is exactly $d$. For the Klee--Minty cube the outmap is
\[
  s(b)=\bigl\{\,i\ :\ b_i\equiv b_{i+1}+\cdots+b_d \pmod 2\,\bigr\},
\]
independently of $\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)$, with sink $(0,\dots,0,1)$; this was
checked against the objective values for $d\le8$. So on these cubes the
bound of \Cref{thm:hcube-dprod} is attained.
\end{proposition}

\begin{remark}\label{rem:hcube-km}
The table separates the two questions completely.
\[
\begin{array}{lccc}
\text{family} & d & \text{longest monotone path} & h_{\mathrm{BA}}\\ \hline
\text{Klee--Minty }(\varepsilon=1/4) & 2..12 & 2^{d}-1 & d\\
\text{Klee--Minty }(\varepsilon=1/10) & 2..12 & 2^{d}-1 & d\\
\text{Klee--Minty, Chv\'atal's form} & 2..10 & 2^{d}-1 & d\\
\text{Goldfarb--Sit rescaling} & 2..12 & 2^{d}-1 & d
\end{array}
\]
Every deformed cube is LP-hard-capable and bottom-antipodally trivial, and
\Cref{thm:hcube-dprod} says this is not an accident of the constants: it is
forced by the shape of the definition. A deformed product may only chain its
factors' \emph{heights} additively, so no family of deformed products with
factors of bounded dimension has superlinear bottom-antipodal height. Since
\Cref{def:hcube-deformed} is the standard machine for producing long monotone
paths on cubes --- Klee--Minty, Goldfarb, Goldfarb--Sit, and the
Amenta--Ziegler deformed products that give maximal shadows --- the whole
classical arsenal is useless for \Cref{cor:f-auso}'s pivot, and a
superpolynomial all-switches family must be built by something else. The
attribution of \Cref{def:hcube-deformed} to Amenta and Ziegler, and of the
cubes to Klee and Minty, to Chv\'atal, and to Goldfarb and Sit, is from memory
and unchecked against the sources; the theorem does not depend on the constants
of any particular one of them.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}\label{rem:hcube-notallcubes}
\Cref{thm:hcube-dprod} does not apply to the occupancy polytope $X(G)$ of
\Cref{prop:oneplayer-lp}, and it must not. The proof produces, in every deformed
product, a block of coordinates on which the orientation does not depend on the
rest; for a deformed \emph{cube} that block is a single \emph{uniform}
coordinate, all of whose edges point the same way. A uniform coordinate forces
$h_{\mathrm{BA}}\le1+h^{\ast}(m-1)$, because one bottom-antipodal step carries
every vertex into the facet the coordinate points to and the walk never leaves
it. At $m=4$ that ceiling is $1+h^{\ast}(3)=5$, whereas one-player stopping
games with $|\Vmax|=4$ and an all-switches run of length $6$ exist
(\Cref{prop:hcube-oneplayer}). So their improvement orientation is not the LP
orientation of any deformed cube, and the geometry of $X(G)$ is genuinely
outside \Cref{def:hcube-deformed}.
\end{remark}

\section{The Holt--Klee ceiling at five coordinates}\label{sec:hcube-hk}

\begin{proposition}[$h^{\ast}_{\mathrm{HK}}(5)=11$]\label{prop:hcube-hkfive}
No Holt--Klee acyclic unique sink orientation of the $5$-cube has a
bottom-antipodal walk of length $12$, and some Holt--Klee acyclic unique sink
orientation of the $5$-cube has one of length $11$; an explicit witness is
\[
  \begin{aligned}
  s=(&7,14,28,13,24,25,26,27,15,16,17,22,19,4,5,18,\\
     &30,29,0,31,3,10,12,9,23,2,8,1,11,20,21,6),
  \end{aligned}
\]
whose bottom-antipodal walk from $\sigma_0=0$ is
$0,7,28,23,30,11,29,9,25,27,26,18$. Hence
\[
  h^{\ast}_{\mathrm{HK}}(m)=1,\;2,\;4,\;6,\;11\qquad(m=1,\dots,5),
\]
against $h^{\ast}(m)=1,2,4,7,12$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
By \Cref{lem:auso-laws} every bottom-antipodal trace obeys \Cref{cor:no-return}
and \Cref{cor:law-b}, and both laws are translation invariant, so
$\sigma_0=0$ may be assumed. The $347640$ law-abiding sequences of length $12$
on the $5$-cube were enumerated as in \Cref{prop:hstar-five}; for each, the
outmap was fixed on the $13$ vertices of the trace and completed over the
remaining $19$ by depth-first search under the Szab\'o--Welzl condition, with a
prune firing as soon as a face of dimension $3$ or $4$ became fully assigned
and failed acyclicity, the unique source/sink condition, or the Holt--Klee
count of internally vertex-disjoint monotone source-to-sink paths. The prune is
sound: every face of a Holt--Klee acyclic unique sink orientation is acyclic,
has a unique sink, has a unique source (the reversal of a unique sink
orientation is one), and is Holt--Klee. No completion survived. The same
program with the Holt--Klee prune switched off reproduces
\Cref{prop:hstar-five}'s witness outmap $(15,0,1,2,27,30,12,\dots)$ from the
same trace $0,15,24,31,20,23,18,\dots$, which is the check on the enumeration;
with the prune on and length $11$ it returns the displayed orientation after
$73266$ sequences. That orientation was then re-verified independently: the
outmap is a bijection, the Szab\'o--Welzl condition holds on all $496$ pairs,
the orientation is acyclic, its bottom-antipodal heights are
$(11,7,8,8,10,10,10,10,11,4,3,6,5,5,7,6,8,6,0,6,9,5,2,8,7,3,1,2,9,5,7,4)$ with
maximum $11$, and the Holt--Klee maximum flow succeeds on all $51$ faces of
dimension at least three (the $2$-faces of a unique sink orientation are
automatic).

The Holt--Klee test is a unit vertex-capacity maximum flow computed by
Ford--Fulkerson with breadth-first augmentation and residual arcs on the
vertex-split graph of each face. It was validated by recomputing, from an
independent enumeration, the census of \Cref{prop:auso-census}: $12$ unique
sink orientations of the $2$-cube, all acyclic and all Holt--Klee; $744$ of the
$3$-cube, $728$ acyclic in $18$ classes, $656$ Holt--Klee in $16$ classes; and
on the orientation of \Cref{prop:auso-seven} it returns $2$ disjoint paths
where $4$ are needed, with the same failing $3$-face (directions $1,2,4$ at the
vertex $4$) that \Cref{cor:seven-two-player} names.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{rem:hcube-hkfive}
This confirms the measurement recorded as unverified. Two consequences. First,
$h^{\ast}_{\mathrm{HK}}$ is not merely $h^{\ast}$ with the top removed: it loses
one at $m=4$ and one at $m=5$, and the losses are independent computations.
Second, the numbers leave room for a doubling: $11\ge2\cdot4+2$, so nothing in
the table forbids an operation raising the dimension by two and at least
doubling the height \emph{inside} the Holt--Klee class, which is what an
LP-realisable exponential family would need. \Cref{sec:hcube-blow} shows that
\Cref{thm:blowup}'s $B$ is not such an operation and says exactly which face
stops it.
\end{remark}

\section{One-player heights and LP realisability}\label{sec:hcube-one}

Write $h^{\ast}_1(m)$ for the greatest length of an all-switches run of a
one-player stopping SSG with $|\Vmax|=m$ and no tied incidence, and
$h^{\ast}_{\mathrm{LP}}(m)$ for the greatest bottom-antipodal height of an
orientation induced by a linear objective on a polytope combinatorially
equivalent to the $m$-cube. By \Cref{prop:oneplayer-lp} and Holt--Klee,
\[
  h^{\ast}_1(m)\ \le\ h^{\ast}_{\mathrm{LP}}(m)\ \le\ h^{\ast}_{\mathrm{HK}}(m)
   \ \le\ h^{\ast}(m).
\]

\begin{proposition}[Explicit one-player runs]\label{prop:hcube-oneplayer}
Let a one-player stopping game be presented by its harmonic normal form: for
each $v\in\Vmax$ and each action $a$ a row of nonnegative integers
$(p^{v,a}_1,\dots,p^{v,a}_m,q^{v,a})$ over a denominator $D$ with
$\sum_jp^{v,a}_j+q^{v,a}<D$, the missing mass leaking to $t_0$. Then there are
such games, with no tied incidence, whose all-switches runs have length
\[
  h^{\ast}_1(3)\ge4,\quad h^{\ast}_1(4)\ge6,\quad h^{\ast}_1(5)\ge9,\quad
  h^{\ast}_1(6)\ge12 ,
\]
and $h^{\ast}_1$ is non-decreasing --- adjoin a Max vertex whose two actions go
to $t_0$ and to a fresh average vertex of value strictly between the sinks, and
which no other vertex sees: the game stays stopping and nondegenerate, and the
all-switches run is unchanged because the new coordinate is switched, if at all,
in the first round and in parallel --- so $h^{\ast}_1(m)\ge12$ for every
$m\ge6$.
At $m=5$, $D=4096$ and the rows
\[
\begin{array}{lll}
